entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Łaski, the elder (c. 1456 – May 29, 1531), was a towering figure in late medieval Polish governance and a pivotal architect of its legal framework. As Grand Chancellor of the Crown from 1503 to 1510, and a seasoned diplomat, he operated at the very apex of the Jagiellonian monarchy, shaping the political and legal landscape of a vast and evolving Commonwealth. His career, spanning from a secretary to King Casimir IV Jagiellon in 1490 to his later ecclesiastical roles, firmly placed him at the intersection of royal power, noble aspirations, and the codification of national law, making him indispensable to understanding the Polish state's transition into the early modern era.

Łaski's most enduring achievement was the compilation and publication of *Communes privilegia Regni Poloniae* (Latin for 'Common Privileges of the Kingdom of Poland'), popularly known as *Laski's Statutes*, in 1506. This monumental codification, authorized by the Sejm, gathered all existing laws, statutes, and noble privileges into a single, accessible volume, comprising 120 chapters. It served not only as a comprehensive legal reference but also as a political manifesto, solidifying the *szlachta's* (nobility's) dominant position, particularly through the inclusion of the *Nihil novi* constitution of 1505, which prohibited the king from enacting new laws without noble consent. His diplomatic missions, including negotiations with Muscovy and the Ottoman Empire, further underscored his influence in foreign policy under King Sigismund I the Old.

entities.summary:
Jan Łaski (1456–1531), a preeminent Polish nobleman and ecclesiastical statesman, profoundly shaped the legal and political landscape of the Kingdom of Poland during the pivotal late Jagiellonian era. As Grand Chancellor of the Crown from 1503 to 1510, he orchestrated critical legislative reforms, most notably the codification of Polish law in the "Commune Inclyti Regni Poloniae Privilegium" (known as the Łaski Statute) in 1506. His career traversed the reigns of three Jagiellonian monarchs—Casimir IV, John I Albert, and Alexander Jagiellon—positioning him as a central figure in the consolidation of noble power and the development of a unique parliamentary monarchy in Central Europe amidst the burgeoning Renaissance.

Łaski's early career saw him serving as secretary to King Casimir IV Jagiellon from 1490, a period that honed his legal acumen and political understanding. His ascent to the Grand Chancellorship in 1503 under King Alexander marked the zenith of his administrative influence. During this tenure, he played a crucial role in drafting the Nihil Novi constitution of 1505, which significantly curtailed royal power and established the principle that no new laws could be passed without the consent of the Sejm (parliament). His crowning achievement, the Łaski Statute of 1506, compiled all existing Polish laws, privileges, and statutes into a single, accessible document, comprising 150 articles and 500 pages. This monumental work, published in Latin and Polish, standardized legal practice and served as the foundational legal text for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth for centuries.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan Łaski's compilation of the Łaski Statute and his role in the Nihil Novi Act fundamentally structured Polish law and governance for centuries, establishing a unique parliamentary monarchy and solidifying noble privileges. His work provided the legal foundation for the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth's distinct political system.
